name: Horizons Math
line: In Horizons Math a parent teaches and grades a daily lesson. In AMP, teaching and checking happen at every problem.
description: AMP vs Horizons Math: a parent teaches and grades a daily lesson from the book. In AMP, assessment, teaching and review are continuous, at every problem.
verdict: Horizons Math is a print series in which a parent teaches a daily lesson from the teacher's guide, grades the pages with the answer key, and follows the book's spiral order [1]. In AMP, assessment and teaching are continuous. Every answer updates the learner's level and sets the next problem, and each problem carries its own hint, lesson and worked answer.

reasons.title: Continuous assessment
reasons.body: AMP has no separate test. It places a learner from their first answers, and every answer after updates the learner's level in that part of math and sets the next problem: new work within reach, a gap to close, or an old skill due back. Horizons places a child with a printed readiness test that the parent scores from an answer key [2]. After that, the lessons come in the book's order, the same for every child [1].

reasons.title: The problem is the unit
reasons.body: In AMP, everything a learner needs hangs off the problem in front of them: a hint that gives the first step, a lesson with a worked example, a video lesson, the worked answer afterward, and links to the skills it builds on and leads to. In Horizons the unit is the daily lesson. The parent teaches it from the teacher's guide, one-on-one, and the child works the matching workbook pages [1][5]. Across 55 studies, worked examples improve performance in math [11].

reasons.title: Feedback on every answer
reasons.body: After each answer AMP shows whether it was right, the correct answer and the worked steps, then the next problem. In Horizons the child works the pages and the parent grades them afterward with the answer key [1]. Across 40 studies of computer feedback, feedback that explains had the largest average effect [10].

reasons.title: Continuous review
reasons.body: In AMP, learned skills come back in ordinary practice, at growing intervals, mixed with other math. Horizons is a spiral: concepts are repeatedly revisited as new, related ones are introduced, in the book's order [1]. In a randomized trial with 787 seventh graders, mixed and spaced practice scored 62% a month later on the researchers' own test, against 38% for practice in blocks [9].

reasons.title: Moving on, and going back
reasons.body: In AMP a skill counts as learned when the learner gets it right without help, more than once. An answer after a hint or a lesson is marked as helped. Repeated misses send practice back to what the skill builds on. AOP contrasts Horizons' spiral with mastery-based learning, and the parent decides when to reteach [1].

rows.range: Kindergarten through grade 6, then Pre-Algebra and Algebra I. AOP points families to its other programs for high school [1][4].
rows.start: A printable readiness test, scored by the parent from an answer key [2].
rows.teaching: A daily lesson the parent teaches from the teacher's guide, one-on-one, with hands-on activities [1][5].
rows.next: The next lesson in the book, in a fixed spiral order, the same for every child [1].
rows.mastery: No mastery rule. AOP describes Horizons as spiral rather than mastery-based [1].
rows.review: Spiral: concepts are revisited as new, related ones are introduced, in the book's order [1].
rows.print: Print is the whole program: workbooks, one set per child with the same pages for every child, and a teacher's guide with answer keys [1][5][6].
rows.adult: Teaches the daily lesson, grades the pages with the answer key, and decides when to reteach [1].
rows.reports: The parent's own grades from the answer key [1].
rows.evidence: We found no entry in Evidence for ESSA [7] and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [8]. Its Horizons page cites no research [1].

theirs: Horizons Math is published by Alpha Omega Publications (AOP), a Christian homeschool publisher [3]. It is a print series that runs from kindergarten through grade 6, then Pre-Algebra and Algebra I [1][4]. A grade comes as two student workbooks and a teacher's guide [5][6].

Each day the parent teaches a lesson from the guide, one-on-one, often with hands-on activities that use household items. The child works the matching workbook pages, and the parent grades them with the answer key [1][5]. The guide also holds a daily planner, teaching tips and extra worksheets [6]. AOP calls the design spiral: concepts are revisited as new, related ones are introduced [1].
credit: A spiral that brings concepts back as new, related ones arrive [1].
A parent at the table, teaching one-on-one with hands-on activities [5].
Printable readiness tests to place a child before the first lesson [2].

theirs: We found no outcome study of Horizons Math on AOP's Horizons page, in Evidence for ESSA, or in What Works Clearinghouse intervention reports as of November 2026 [1][7][8]. The clearinghouse's report titled Direct Instruction/Horizons covers an SRA reading program, a different product [8]. AOP's Horizons page cites no research or efficacy data [1].
ours: Two findings bear on this comparison. Across 40 studies of computer-based feedback, feedback that explains averaged an effect of 0.49, against 0.32 for giving the correct answer and 0.05 for marking right or wrong only [10]. These are averages by feedback type, not a head-to-head trial. Across 55 studies in math, worked examples averaged g = 0.48 [11]. AMP applies both at every problem.

AMP's own outcome studies are planned: growth on a national test against hours of use, then comparison groups, then randomized trials. Each will be registered before it starts and published whatever it finds. The research behind each part of AMP is in our report, and AMP is open source.

them: You want to teach each math lesson yourself, one-on-one, from a book.
amp: You want assessment, teaching and review in the same practice, with no separate tests.
You want every answer checked as it is given, with the worked steps.
You want learned skills to keep coming back in ordinary practice.
Your learner is at different levels in different parts of math.
You want daily practice with no lesson to plan, teach or grade.

questions.question: How is AMP different from Horizons Math?
questions.answer: In Horizons Math a parent teaches each day's lesson from the guide and grades the pages with the answer key, and concepts return in the book's spiral order [1]. AMP has no separate test: every answer sets the next problem, each problem carries its own teaching, and learned skills return in ordinary practice.

questions.question: Does Horizons Math work?
questions.answer: We found no outcome study in the pages we read. Horizons Math has no entry in Evidence for ESSA and no What Works Clearinghouse intervention report [7][8], and its own page cites no research [1].

questions.question: Can a learner use both?
questions.answer: Yes. They are separate programs. A parent can keep teaching Horizons lessons, and AMP places the learner from their first answers, whatever book they are in.
